invariant_bindings.invariant_text: Session ids MUST carry >=128 bits of CSPRNG entropy and MUST NEVER encode user-controlled input.
On privilege elevation the session id MUST be rotated; the prior id CANNOT be reused.
Sessions MUST expire at min(idle, absolute); server-side revocation MUST win over client-held cookies.
Session cookies MUST be Secure + HttpOnly + SameSite in {Lax, Strict}; Domain SHALL NEVER be broader than the application host.
revoke_all_for_subject MUST terminate every live session for that subject atomically and MUST be invoked on password change.
load() MUST NEVER extend a session past absolute_expires_at even on sustained activity.

tier_reports.summary: mypy --strict clean; ruff (curated ALL) clean; 0 suppressions all rationale-attached.
LLM judge ≥8/10 on six axes; all five personas understood the docs.

attacks.hypothesis: If create() uses random.random() or time-seeded Mersenne Twister instead of secrets.token_bytes, generated ids may have <128 bits of effective entropy and be predictable from a few observed sessions, violating entropy invariant.
attacks.input_fixture: Call create('alice') 1000 times; analyze ids for Mersenne Twister state recovery via 624 consecutive 32-bit outputs.

attacks.hypothesis: Implementation may concatenate subject into session id (e.g. f'{subject}-{rand}'), leaking subject and allowing crafted subject strings to collide or inject separators, violating the no-user-controlled-input rule.
attacks.input_fixture: create(subject='admin\x00../etc/passwd'); inspect returned Session.id for subject substring.

attacks.hypothesis: After rotate(old_id), load(old_id) may still return the session (soft rotation) allowing fixation: attacker who captured the pre-login id keeps valid access post-privilege-elevation.
attacks.input_fixture: s1=create('u'); new=rotate(s1.id); assert load(s1.id) is None  # expected to fail

attacks.hypothesis: Concurrent rotate(id) calls from two threads may both succeed and yield two distinct valid successor ids, splitting the session and letting an attacker retain one branch.
attacks.input_fixture: s=create('u'); Thread(target=rotate,args=(s.id,)) x2; count resulting live sessions — expect exactly 1.

attacks.hypothesis: load() may refresh idle_expires_at past absolute_expires_at when now > absolute, returning a live session and violating the hard ceiling.
attacks.input_fixture: freeze_time to absolute_expires_at+1; load(s.id) — expect None, attack asserts it returns Session.

attacks.hypothesis: If created_at uses time.time() and a later load uses monotonic or system clock moves backward (NTP step), idle_expires_at comparison may wrap making session immortal.
attacks.input_fixture: Mock time.time() to return created_at-10000 on load; expect still-expiring behavior, attack shows infinite life.

attacks.hypothesis: Passing absolute_timeout=2**63 during create may overflow int64 when added to created_at, wrapping to negative and making every load() return None — or worse, wrap to huge positive making session effectively permanent.
attacks.input_fixture: create('u', absolute_timeout=2**63-1); inspect absolute_expires_at sign.

attacks.hypothesis: revoke_all_for_subject iterates and deletes one-by-one without a transaction; a session created mid-iteration survives password-change revocation, leaving a live attacker session.
attacks.input_fixture: Thread A: revoke_all_for_subject('u'); Thread B: create('u') interleaved. Count live sessions after — expect 0.

attacks.hypothesis: revoke(id) removes from backing store but load() reads from an in-process LRU cache without invalidation, so client cookie keeps working until TTL — server-side revocation does NOT win.
attacks.input_fixture: s=create('u'); load(s.id); revoke(s.id); load(s.id) — expect None, attack shows Session.

attacks.hypothesis: load(None) or load(b'\x00'*32) or load({'$gt':''}) may raise uncaught exception or — in a Mongo-backed store — return the first session via NoSQL injection.
attacks.input_fixture: load({'$ne': None}); load(None); load('../' * 500)

attacks.hypothesis: load() compares ids with == (short-circuit) rather than constant-time; attacker measures response time to recover valid id byte-by-byte, reducing effective entropy below 128 bits.
attacks.input_fixture: Run 1e6 load() calls with ids differing at position 0,1,2... measure timing deltas > 50ns.

attacks.hypothesis: Cookie serialization helper defaults Domain to eTLD+1 (e.g. .example.com) broader than app host app.example.com, letting sibling subdomains (evil.example.com) read the session cookie.
attacks.input_fixture: Issue session for host app.example.com; inspect Set-Cookie header for Domain=.example.com.

attacks.hypothesis: Under a 'cross_site_embed' config flag, library emits SameSite=None without Secure, or downgrades to no SameSite attribute in legacy-browser mode, enabling CSRF session riding.
attacks.input_fixture: Configure store with legacy_compat=True; inspect Set-Cookie — expect SameSite=Lax, attack shows missing.

attacks.hypothesis: After revoke_all_for_subject('alice'), a captured pre-revocation session id is replayed and load() returns a freshly-issued session for a different user 'alice' created seconds later (subject-key collision).
attacks.input_fixture: s1=create('alice'); revoke_all_for_subject('alice'); s2=create('alice'); load(s1.id) — expect None.

attacks.hypothesis: create('') or create(None) produces a session with empty subject; revoke_all_for_subject('') then nukes every anonymous/guest session across tenants — amplification DoS.
attacks.input_fixture: for _ in 10000: create(''); revoke_all_for_subject('') — observe mass termination.

attacks.hypothesis: create() logs the generated session id at INFO level for 'audit', leaking the bearer token into log aggregation where any ops engineer can replay it.
attacks.input_fixture: Capture logging output during create('u'); grep for session.id substring.

attacks.hypothesis: If the create() implementation naively concatenates subject into the session id (e.g. f'{subject}_{secrets.token_hex(8)}'), an attacker who controls their own subject string can predict or enumerate session ids for other subjects by observing the format, and the user-controlled prefix also reduces effective entropy below 128 bits.
attacks.input_fixture: store.create(subject='admin'); inspect returned Session.id for substring match with 'admin'. Also call store.create(subject='A'*200) and verify id does not contain the subject string anywhere.

attacks.hypothesis: After rotate() invalidates old_id and issues new_id, a race window may exist in which a concurrent load(old_id) still succeeds if the backing store uses eventual-consistency or a read replica. The old id should be immediately and durably revoked before rotate() returns.
attacks.input_fixture: Thread-1: s = store.create('bob'); Thread-2: store.rotate(s.id) [blocks at network call]; Thread-1 simultaneously: store.load(s.id) — expect None but may get live Session if deletion is async.

attacks.hypothesis: rotate() may re-derive absolute_expires_at as now()+ABSOLUTE_TTL rather than preserving the original created_at-relative deadline. An attacker who triggers repeated rotations (e.g. via MFA re-challenges) can extend a session indefinitely, bypassing the absolute timeout.
attacks.input_fixture: s0 = store.create('alice'); original_abs = s0.absolute_expires_at; for _ in range(100): s0 = store.rotate(s0.id); assert s0.absolute_expires_at == original_abs  # should not drift forward

attacks.hypothesis: load() implementations that refresh idle_expires_at on every call may accidentally also advance absolute_expires_at if both timestamps are stored as offsets from 'now' rather than as fixed epoch values. Calling load() repeatedly near the absolute boundary would silently extend the session.
attacks.input_fixture: s = store.create('carol'); freeze time to absolute_expires_at - 1; store.load(s.id); advance clock by 2 seconds; result = store.load(s.id); assert result is None  # must be expired, not refreshed

attacks.hypothesis: revoke_all_for_subject() may enumerate sessions and delete them one-by-one in a loop. A concurrent create() call for the same subject between the enumeration snapshot and the final delete can insert a new session that survives the revocation, leaving the subject with a live session after a password change.
attacks.input_fixture: Thread-1: store.revoke_all_for_subject('dave') [patched to sleep 50ms between deletes]; Thread-2: store.create('dave') [fires during the sleep]; after Thread-1 finishes, store.load of Thread-2 session id should return None but may return a live Session.

attacks.hypothesis: If the deployment environment exhausts /dev/urandom or the CSPRNG raises an exception (e.g. in a sandboxed container on first boot), a naive implementation may silently fall back to random.random() or uuid4() seeded from time.time(), dropping to ~32 bits of effective entropy and making session ids predictable.
attacks.input_fixture: Mock os.urandom to raise BlockingIOError; call store.create('eve'); measure bit-entropy of 10000 generated ids via Shannon entropy — expect >= 128 bits; if fallback exists, entropy collapses to ~32 bits.

attacks.hypothesis: If revoke() marks the session deleted in a primary store but a caching layer (Redis, in-memory dict) still holds a non-expired copy, load() served from cache will return the revoked session, meaning server-side revocation does NOT win over the client-held cookie.
attacks.input_fixture: s = store.create('frank'); store.revoke(s.id); result = store.load(s.id); assert result is None — if cache invalidation is missing, result will be the original live Session.

attacks.hypothesis: If the cookie Domain attribute is derived from a Host header or a configurable base_url string without strict validation, an attacker-controlled Host: .evil.example.com header could cause the server to issue a session cookie scoped to .evil.example.com, allowing subdomain session hijacking.
attacks.input_fixture: HTTP request with header 'Host: .attacker.example.com'; observe Set-Cookie response header; Domain= attribute must NOT begin with a dot broader than the application's registered hostname.

attacks.hypothesis: If the SameSite attribute is conditionally omitted or set to None when the request's User-Agent is detected as an older browser (SameSite=None compatibility shim), cross-site requests from an attacker-controlled origin can include the session cookie, enabling CSRF despite the declared SameSite=Lax/Strict invariant.
attacks.input_fixture: Send request with User-Agent matching a UA blocklist (e.g. Chrome 51 or Safari 12); inspect Set-Cookie for SameSite attribute; if absent or 'None' without Secure, cross-origin iframe POST will include the cookie.

attacks.hypothesis: If expiry comparisons use wall-clock time and the server clock jumps backward (NTP correction or VM migration), a session that was absolute-expired and revoked may appear unexpired again. A replayed old session cookie could be accepted by load() because absolute_expires_at > now() after the clock rollback.
attacks.input_fixture: s = store.create('grace'); advance mock clock to absolute_expires_at + 1; verify load returns None; roll clock BACK 10 seconds (simulating NTP correction); call store.load(s.id) again — must still return None; revocation must be durable, not clock-relative.

attacks.hypothesis: The invariant requires revoke_all_for_subject() to be invoked on password change, but if the SessionStore is a library primitive it cannot enforce its own invocation. A missing integration test means password-change flows may update credentials without calling revoke_all, leaving all prior sessions live for an attacker who stole them before the password change.
attacks.input_fixture: Audit password-change handler code path: grep for revoke_all_for_subject in auth controller; simulate password change via API, then call store.load(old_session_id) — must return None; if integration is absent, old session survives.

attacks.hypothesis: If load() accepts a caller-supplied session_id without verifying that the id was generated by the store itself (e.g. no HMAC prefix, no registry lookup), an attacker can pre-seed a known id into the store via a crafted create() call using a predictable subject, then socially engineer the victim into authenticating with that id, achieving session fixation.
attacks.input_fixture: attacker_session = store.create('anonymous'); send attacker_session.id to victim as a login link parameter; victim authenticates and the server calls rotate(attacker_session.id) — if rotate preserves the attacker-known id as a reachable alias or the store allows unauthenticated id injection, fixation succeeds.

attacks.hypothesis: If created_at, idle_expires_at, or absolute_expires_at are stored as 32-bit integers (Unix epoch), they will overflow in 2038. A session created with a TTL that causes absolute_expires_at to exceed 2^31-1 will wrap to a negative or near-zero timestamp, making the session appear already-expired on creation or immortal depending on comparison direction.
attacks.input_fixture: store.create subject='henry' with absolute_timeout=datetime(2039,1,1); inspect Session.absolute_expires_at — if stored as int32, value wraps to negative; store.load should return None immediately but wrapping makes it appear expired already OR the comparison `now < absolute` fails in the wrong direction.

attacks.hypothesis: Calling create('') or create(None) when subject validation is absent may produce a session with an empty-string subject. revoke_all_for_subject('') would then delete sessions for ALL subjects whose subject field happens to match the empty default, or a None comparison may cause a wildcard match in certain ORM queries (e.g. WHERE subject = NULL being true for all NULLs), deleting every session in the store.
attacks.input_fixture: store.create('ivan'); store.create('julia'); store.create(''); store.revoke_all_for_subject(''); verify store.load of ivan and julia sessions are NOT None — if ORM emits 'DELETE WHERE subject IS NULL' instead of 'WHERE subject = \"\"', all sessions may be wiped.

attacks.hypothesis: SessionStore uses system PRNG instead of CSPRNG, generating only 64-bit entropy; attacker brute-forces 2^64 session IDs in seconds.
attacks.input_fixture: create('user1'); measure entropy of returned session_id; if entropy < 128 bits, attacker can enumerate all valid sessions

attacks.hypothesis: Session ID structure encodes user_id as plaintext prefix (e.g., base64(user_id || nonce)); user_id is public; attacker predicts subsequent nonces.
attacks.input_fixture: observe session_ids from create('alice'), create('bob'); decode to reveal user names; guess nonce sequence; predict valid session_ids for other users

attacks.hypothesis: Privilege escalation event (login, MFA step-up) does not trigger rotate(); attacker uses pre-privilege session_id post-escalation.
attacks.input_fixture: [Attacker] create('victim'); [Victim logs in]; [No rotate() called]; load(attacker_sid) succeeds with elevated privileges

attacks.hypothesis: rotate() returns session_id from a pool of previously-used IDs instead of generating fresh entropy; attacker reuses old ID after rotation.
attacks.input_fixture: sid1 = create(); sid2 = rotate(sid1); sid3 = rotate(sid2); if sid3 in [sid1, sid2], attacker can fixate on recycled ID

attacks.hypothesis: load() refreshes absolute_expires_at on each access; repeated activity within idle_timeout extends session indefinitely past absolute deadline.
attacks.input_fixture: s = create(idle_timeout=1h, absolute_timeout=1h); load(s.id) @ 0:30; load(s.id) @ 1:00; load(s.id) @ 1:30; absolute_expires_at keeps advancing

attacks.hypothesis: Server-side revoke(sid) succeeds; client-held cookie still contains sid; attacker replays sid in next request; load(sid) succeeds.
attacks.input_fixture: revoke(sid); [attacker retains sid from Set-Cookie header]; construct HTTP request with Cookie: sessionid=sid; load(sid) succeeds

attacks.hypothesis: Set-Cookie header omits Secure flag; session_id transmitted over HTTP; network attacker on same LAN captures plaintext session_id.
attacks.input_fixture: Set-Cookie: sessionid=XXXXX (no Secure flag); HTTP request over unencrypted channel; tcpdump reveals session_id in plaintext

attacks.hypothesis: revoke_all_for_subject() checks live sessions then proceeds to delete; attacker's concurrent create() between check and delete survives revocation.
attacks.input_fixture: [Thread A] revoke_all_for_subject('user1'); [Thread B interleaves] create('user1') before delete completes; new_sid remains valid

attacks.hypothesis: Expiry checks use system clock without monotonicity guards; attacker sets system clock backward; expired sessions become valid again.
attacks.input_fixture: create(absolute_timeout=1h); await 65 minutes; load(sid) returns None; [system clock -90 minutes]; load(sid) succeeds

attacks.hypothesis: SessionStore allows idle_timeout=0; session expires immediately but load() still returns valid Session object instead of None.
attacks.input_fixture: create('user', idle_timeout=0, absolute_timeout=3600); immediate load(sid) succeeds; session should already be expired

attacks.hypothesis: absolute_expires_at stored as signed 64-bit int; value set to 2^63-100 causes overflow in age calculation; session never expires.
attacks.input_fixture: create('user', absolute_timeout=2^63-100); absolute_expires_at overflows; comparison (absolute_expires_at - current_time) yields negative; session valid forever

attacks.hypothesis: SessionStore accepts 127-bit entropy (just below 128-bit requirement); birthday paradox collision occurs at 2^63.5 sessions instead of 2^64.
attacks.input_fixture: SessionStore configured with 127-bit CSPRNG; generate 2^64 sessions concurrently; probabilistic session_id collision observed

attacks.hypothesis: revoke_all_for_subject() returns immediately after local cache clear but before replication; read-replica still returns revoked sessions.
attacks.input_fixture: revoke_all_for_subject('user1'); [attacker reads from asynchronous replica immediately]; load(old_sid) succeeds on replica before sync completes

axes.rationale: Protocol surface matches api_signature verbatim (create/load/rotate/revoke/revoke_all_for_subject returning correct types). Session dataclass fields and types match. Frozen dataclass per spec. Invariant IDs in code use hyphen form (SESSION-INV-01) vs spec underscore (SESSION_INV_01) — minor cosmetic drift but same semantics.

All six invariants implemented: CSPRNG minting with entropy floor, rotation with tombstone, dual-clock min expiry with revocation precedence, cookie Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite/Domain validation, subject-wide revocation, absolute ceiling respected on sliding renew and rotate. Extension gate via register_adapter. Constant-time comparator included. Missing: no observability hooks emitted in-module (spec says wired by web layer, so acceptable).

Single typed SessionInvariantError; every raise cites the specific SESSION-INV-0N id and explains the violation. Load returns None on invalid input rather than raising (correct for cookie path). Rotate raises on unknown/revoked/expired with distinct messages. Collision detection refuses rather than overwrites.

runtime_checkable Protocol lets adapters bind structurally. Session value object is frozen/slots and reusable by redis/postgres adapters. clock and id_factory injection points enable deterministic tests. CookieConfig is framework-agnostic. register_adapter enforces capability contract. No hidden global state; zero I/O at import.

threading.RLock serialises mutations; rotate is wins-one atomic via lock + collision check; revoke_all is atomic under lock. Tombstone set prevents replay. Sliding renew capped at absolute ceiling. CSPRNG via secrets. Constant-time compare. No logging/metrics emission here (delegated), but memory growth of _revoked_ids is unbounded over time — no TTL/cleanup — a real concern for long-lived processes.

Namespace auth, Protocol + Session dataclass match api_signature exactly. Invariant texts echo catalog wording. Extension contract enforced via register_adapter matching spec's forbidden-binding clause. Alternatives and maturity align with docs. Minor: invariant id formatting (hyphen vs underscore) diverges from spec table, but bindings doc referenced separately.

friction_points: 'privilege elevation' and 'session fixation' appear in the first paragraph with no plain-language gloss — a junior dev must already know these terms to understand the opening sentence.
The six-row invariant table appears before the code example; a reader who has never used the API has no anchor for what SESSION_INV_02 is protecting against.
'tombstoned' and 'CSPRNG' in the lifecycle and security sections are left unexplained, breaking reading flow for anyone without a security background.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Move the Usage section directly after 'What it does'; inline a one-line definition for 'privilege elevation' (e.g., step-up auth such as MFA or role change) and 'session fixation' (attacker plants a known id before login) on first use; annotate the state machine with plain-English callouts and replace bare 'tombstoned' with 'permanently invalidated (tombstoned)'.

friction_points: The valid capability flag names for register_adapter() are never listed — an engineer writing a Redis adapter cannot know the accepted enum values without reading source.

The exact Protocol surface (abstract method signatures with types) that adapters must satisfy is absent; the extension contract section describes behavior in prose but provides no interface definition.
File paths for SessionStore.contract.json, invariant_bindings.json, and SessionStore.tla are not given; a reader wanting to verify TLA+ properties or API signatures has no path to start from.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add an 'Adapter Protocol' fenced code block showing the abstract class or Protocol with typed method signatures; list every valid capability string (e.g., SERVER_SIDE_REVOCATION, SUBJECT_WIDE_REVOCATION) as a Python literal or table; provide repo-relative paths for all referenced external files.

friction_points: The invariant→test mapping says 'see invariant_bindings.json' but does not inline the three test names per invariant; an auditor verifying coverage must hunt an external file rather than reading the doc.
No threat model table maps attack classes (fixation, replay, cross-device revocation bypass, concurrent rotate race) to the invariant and test that blocks each — the connection must be inferred.
The concurrency guarantee ('wins-one-loser-many') is prose only; neither a test name nor a TLA+ property name (e.g., LiveRevokedDisjoint) is cited inline, leaving the guarantee unanchored.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Inline an 18-row table (6 invariants × 3 test names each); add a 'Threat model' table with columns Attack | Invariant | Mitigating test; cite the matching TLA+ safety property name next to each concurrency claim so an auditor can trace from attack to formal proof in one step.

friction_points: No session cleanup or expiry sweep mechanism is described — it is unclear whether InMemorySessionStore purges expired entries lazily on load() or via a background thread, which directly affects memory growth under load.
observability_schema.json is referenced for metric schemas but label cardinality and units are not shown inline, forcing an on-call engineer to open a second file to write alert rules.
No memory bound or maximum-session-count configuration is mentioned; an SRE cannot determine when InMemorySessionStore becomes unsafe for production without benchmarking from scratch.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Add an 'Operations runbook' subsection covering: expiry sweep strategy (lazy vs. background), memory cap config knob (if any), and two concrete PromQL examples for the alert thresholds already described in prose; inline the four key metric definitions (name, type, labels, unit) rather than deferring entirely to observability_schema.json.

friction_points: 'maturity' is cited as a field in the contract schema but never defined in the doc — a PM cannot tell stakeholders whether this is alpha, beta, or GA without reading a JSON file.
No scale envelope or performance numbers (sessions per second, memory per session, recommended session ceiling) are given, making it impossible to size infrastructure or set delivery expectations.

TLA+ references, SESSION_INV_XX identifiers, invariant_bindings.json, and the provenance/agent section carry no business signal for a PM and obscure the 'When to use' decision the doc is trying to support.
reviews.rewrite_suggestion: Open with a three-field summary card: maturity (e.g., 'GA — production-ready'), scale envelope (e.g., 'suitable for up to ~100k concurrent sessions on a single node'), and integration effort estimate; collapse all formal-verification, invariant-ID, and provenance content into an appendix; add a one-sentence business consequence to each 'When to use' and 'DO NOT USE' bullet.
